case: A 4-month-old boy is brought to a pediatric clinic because his lips turn blue when he feeds or cries. During one episode he became limp and deeply cyanotic, then improved when his mother held his knees to his chest. Physical examination shows a harsh systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border and a single second heart sound. Oxygen saturation is 82% (95 to 100%) on room air. Chest x-ray shows a boot-shaped heart with decreased pulmonary vascular markings. Echocardiography shows a large ventricular septal defect, an aorta that overrides the septum, narrowing of the right ventricular outflow tract, and right ventricular hypertrophy. The diagnosis is tetralogy of Fallot.

questions.stem: The four structural findings on this infant's echocardiogram trace back to one error during septation of the outflow tract. Which of the following developmental errors best explains all four findings?
options: Failure of the endocardial cushions to fuse
Failure of the conotruncal ridges to spiral
Anterosuperior shift of the outflow septum
Excess resorption of the septum primum
approach: List the four findings: VSD, overriding aorta, right ventricular outflow narrowing, right ventricular hypertrophy.
Ask which single shift could narrow the right outflow and leave the aorta sitting over a septal gap.
Match that to displacement of the infundibular (outflow) septum toward the right ventricular side.
questions.why: In tetralogy of Fallot the infundibular (outflow) septum, built largely from neural crest derived conotruncal tissue, is displaced anteriorly and superiorly. This narrows the right ventricular outflow tract and leaves a malaligned ventricular septal defect with the aorta riding over it. Right ventricular hypertrophy follows because the ventricle pumps against the outflow obstruction. One displacement therefore explains all four findings.
whyNot: Endocardial cushion fusion failure produces atrioventricular septal defects (ostium primum ASD, inlet VSD, a common AV valve), classically in trisomy 21. It does not narrow the outflow tract.
Failure of the conotruncal ridges to spiral produces transposition of the great arteries, where the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk from the left.
Correct.
Excess resorption of the septum primum leaves a secundum atrial septal defect, which causes a left-to-right shunt at the atrial level and no outflow obstruction.

questions.stem: A different newborn has tetralogy of Fallot with complete pulmonary atresia. On day 2 of life his cyanosis suddenly worsens because a fetal channel is closing. That channel develops from which embryonic aortic arch?
options: Left sixth aortic arch
Left fourth aortic arch
Third aortic arch
Right fourth aortic arch
approach: With pulmonary atresia, no blood leaves the right ventricle for the lungs, so lung flow must come from the aorta.
The fetal channel that carries aortic blood to the pulmonary artery is the ductus arteriosus, which closes in the first days of life.
Recall that the ductus arteriosus is the distal part of the left sixth aortic arch.
questions.why: When the pulmonary valve is atretic, all pulmonary blood flow in the newborn depends on the ductus arteriosus carrying blood from the aorta into the pulmonary artery. The ductus begins to constrict within hours of birth and usually closes functionally over the first few days as arterial oxygen rises and prostaglandin E2 falls, so lung flow drops and cyanosis worsens. The ductus arteriosus forms from the distal part of the left sixth aortic arch, while the proximal sixth arches form the proximal pulmonary arteries.
whyNot: Correct.
The left fourth arch forms part of the adult arch of the aorta. It does not form a channel that closes after birth.
The third arches form the common carotid arteries and the first part of the internal carotid arteries. They have no role in neonatal pulmonary flow.
The right fourth arch forms the proximal right subclavian artery, a permanent vessel that does not close after birth.

questions.stem: Further testing of the 4-month-old shows a serum calcium of 6.9 mg/dL (8.8 to 10.8 mg/dL), a low parathyroid hormone level, and no thymic shadow on chest x-ray. Which genetic finding is most likely?
options: Trisomy 21 on karyotype
Monosomy X on karyotype
Microdeletion at 7q11.23
Microdeletion at 22q11.2
approach: Group the findings: a conotruncal heart defect, low calcium from low parathyroid hormone, and an absent thymus.
Link parathyroid and thymus loss to failed development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches.
Name the deletion syndrome that combines pouch defects with conotruncal defects.
questions.why: A 22q11.2 microdeletion (DiGeorge syndrome) disrupts neural crest migration and development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches. The pouches form the parathyroid glands and thymus, so infants have hypocalcemia from hypoparathyroidism and T-cell deficiency from thymic hypoplasia. Neural crest cells also build the conotruncal septum, so tetralogy of Fallot and truncus arteriosus are common. The deletion is found by FISH or chromosomal microarray, since it is too small to see on a routine karyotype.
whyNot: Trisomy 21 is most strongly linked to atrioventricular septal defects. It does not cause hypoparathyroidism or an absent thymus.
Monosomy X (Turner syndrome) is linked to coarctation of the aorta and bicuspid aortic valve, with normal parathyroid and thymic development.
A 7q11.23 deletion causes Williams syndrome, with supravalvular aortic stenosis and high, not low, calcium.
Correct.

questions.stem: During the spell described in the case, his color improved when his knees were held to his chest. Which of the following best explains this improvement?
options: It lowered outflow resistance in the narrowed right ventricle
It raised systemic resistance and cut the right-to-left shunt
It reduced venous return and lengthened ventricular filling
It lowered pulmonary resistance and drew blood to the lungs
approach: Shunt direction across the VSD depends on the balance between right ventricular outflow resistance and systemic vascular resistance.
Flexing the legs compresses the femoral arteries and raises systemic vascular resistance.
Higher systemic resistance pushes less blood right to left and sends more right ventricular output through the pulmonary valve.
questions.why: In tetralogy of Fallot, blood leaving the right ventricle chooses between the narrowed outflow tract and the VSD into the aorta. When systemic vascular resistance falls or outflow spasm worsens, more deoxygenated blood shunts right to left and a hypercyanotic spell follows. Pressing the knees to the chest (the infant version of squatting) kinks the femoral arteries and raises systemic vascular resistance, which reduces the right-to-left shunt and sends more blood to the lungs. It also increases venous return to the right heart.
whyNot: Knee-chest positioning does not relax the infundibular obstruction. Drugs such as beta blockers are used to reduce infundibular spasm.
Correct.
Squatting and knee-chest positioning increase venous return from the legs. Reduced venous return would lower right ventricular output to the lungs and would not help.
Knee-chest positioning acts on the systemic side. Pulmonary vascular resistance is already low here, and the fixed outflow narrowing, not pulmonary vascular tone, limits lung flow.

dx: Systemic embolism to the superior mesenteric artery from a left atrial thrombus
case: A 76-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with sudden, severe periumbilical pain that began 3 hours ago. She has atrial fibrillation and stopped taking her anticoagulant 2 months ago. Pulse is 118/min and irregularly irregular, and blood pressure is 142/86 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a soft, mildly tender abdomen, and the pain is out of proportion to these findings. Serum lactate is 5.8 mmol/L (0.5 to 2.2 mmol/L). CT angiography shows an embolus blocking the superior mesenteric artery a few centimeters beyond its origin from the aorta. Echocardiography shows remaining thrombus in the left atrial appendage. The diagnosis is acute mesenteric ischemia from a cardiac embolus.

questions.stem: Given the site where the embolus has lodged, which of the following segments of bowel is most likely to keep its normal arterial supply?
options: Sigmoid colon
Terminal ileum
Ascending colon
Cecum
approach: An embolus in the proximal superior mesenteric artery (SMA) cuts off the branches that arise beyond it.
List the SMA territory: jejunum, ileum, cecum, appendix, ascending colon, and about the proximal two thirds of the transverse colon.
Pick the segment supplied by a different trunk, the inferior mesenteric artery.
questions.why: The SMA supplies midgut structures: the small bowel beyond the duodenum, the cecum and appendix, the ascending colon, and about the proximal two thirds of the transverse colon. The sigmoid colon is hindgut and receives blood from the sigmoid branches of the inferior mesenteric artery, so an SMA embolus leaves it perfused. Knowing the boundary between midgut and hindgut supply predicts which bowel will be ischemic.
whyNot: Correct.
The terminal ileum is supplied by the ileocolic artery, a branch of the SMA, so it is at high risk here.
The ascending colon is supplied by the right colic and ileocolic branches of the SMA, so it is at risk. It would stay perfused if the inferior mesenteric artery were the vessel blocked.
The cecum is supplied by the ileocolic artery from the SMA and is at risk with this embolus.

questions.stem: Which of the following factors is mainly responsible for formation of the thrombus that later broke off and became her embolus?
options: Endothelial injury from a jet of regurgitant blood
Hyperviscosity from an increased red cell mass
Stasis of blood in the poorly emptying appendage
Antibodies against phospholipid-binding proteins
approach: Locate the source: a left atrial appendage thrombus in a patient with atrial fibrillation.
Apply Virchow triad and ask which arm atrial fibrillation disturbs.
Loss of organized atrial contraction leaves blood pooling in the appendage, which is stasis.
questions.why: In atrial fibrillation the atria quiver and no longer contract in an organized way. Blood pools in the left atrial appendage, a blind pouch, and stasis lets clotting factors accumulate and keeps platelets in contact with the wall. A thrombus forms there and pieces can break off into the systemic circulation, where they lodge in the brain, gut, kidneys, spleen, or limbs. This is why anticoagulation is used in atrial fibrillation to prevent stroke and other systemic emboli.
whyNot: Jet lesions from regurgitant valves injure endothelium, but nothing in the case points to valve disease. Endothelial injury is the main factor in arterial thrombosis on a plaque.
Hyperviscosity from polycythemia can promote thrombosis, but nothing in her case suggests a raised red cell mass. Her atrial fibrillation explains the thrombus.
Correct.

Antiphospholipid syndrome causes arterial and venous thrombi, but nothing in the case suggests it, such as lupus, pregnancy losses, or a prolonged PTT. Atrial fibrillation fully explains her thrombus.

questions.stem: Her increased lactate comes from ischemic intestinal cells that keep making ATP through glycolysis without oxygen. Which of the following reactions allows glycolysis to continue in these cells?
options: Oxidation of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA in mitochondria
Reduction of pyruvate to lactate, regenerating NAD+
Conversion of lactate back to glucose in hepatocytes
Transamination of pyruvate to alanine by alanine aminotransferase
approach: Glycolysis needs NAD+ at the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase step.
Without oxygen, the electron transport chain cannot reoxidize NADH.
Lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate to lactate and returns NAD+ so glycolysis can keep running.
questions.why: Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase uses NAD+ and produces NADH. Normally mitochondria reoxidize NADH through the electron transport chain, but that requires oxygen. In ischemic tissue, lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate to lactate and converts NADH back to NAD+, so glycolysis continues and yields a net 2 ATP per glucose. The lactate spills into the blood, which is why a raised serum lactate is a clue to bowel ischemia.
whyNot: Pyruvate dehydrogenase feeds pyruvate into the citric acid cycle. This path depends on oxygen being available to reoxidize NADH and is what fails in ischemia.
Correct.
Gluconeogenesis from lactate (the Cori cycle) happens in the liver and uses ATP. It clears lactate and does not keep glycolysis running in the ischemic gut.
Alanine aminotransferase transfers an amino group from glutamate to pyruvate to make alanine. It does not regenerate NAD+, so it cannot sustain anaerobic glycolysis.

questions.stem: On day 2 she develops fever, hypotension, and leukocytosis after gram-negative bacteria cross the necrotic bowel wall into the blood. Which of the following host recognition events most directly initiates this inflammatory response?
options: Toll-like receptor 2 binding lipoteichoic acid
Toll-like receptor 3 binding double-stranded RNA
Toll-like receptor 9 binding unmethylated CpG DNA
Toll-like receptor 4 binding lipid A
approach: Gram-negative bacteria carry lipopolysaccharide (endotoxin) in their outer membrane.
Lipid A is the toxic part of lipopolysaccharide.
Lipid A is recognized by toll-like receptor 4 (with CD14 and MD-2) on macrophages, which triggers TNF-alpha, IL-1, and IL-6 release.
questions.why: Once the bowel wall dies, gut gram-negative bacteria and their lipopolysaccharide reach the circulation. Lipid A binds the TLR4 complex (with CD14 and MD-2) on macrophages and other innate cells. Signaling through NF-kappa B releases TNF-alpha, IL-1, and IL-6, which cause fever, vasodilation, and leukocytosis and can progress to septic shock.
whyNot: TLR2 recognizes lipoteichoic acid and lipoproteins, typical of gram-positive bacteria. It would be the main receptor in a gram-positive infection.
TLR3 recognizes double-stranded RNA inside endosomes and responds mainly to viral infection.
TLR9 recognizes unmethylated CpG DNA inside endosomes. It contributes to responses against many microbes, but lipid A is the main trigger of gram-negative septic shock.
Correct.

dx: Hemorrhage from a ruptured spleen with hypovolemia
case: A 19-year-old college student is brought to the emergency department 40 minutes after he was tackled during an intramural rugby game. Two weeks ago he had sore throat, fever, fatigue, and swollen posterior cervical lymph nodes, and a heterophile antibody test was positive. He reports left upper quadrant pain and pain at the tip of his left shoulder. Pulse is 124/min, and blood pressure is 88/56 mm Hg. Physical examination shows cool, pale skin and left upper quadrant tenderness. Hemoglobin is 13.6 g/dL (13.5 to 17.5 g/dL). Bedside ultrasound shows a large amount of free fluid in the abdomen. The diagnosis is hemorrhage from a ruptured spleen with hypovolemia.

questions.stem: His heart rate rose within minutes of the bleed. Which of the following changes in the carotid sinus and aortic arch baroreceptor reflex best explains this finding?
options: Increased stretch receptor firing with increased vagal outflow
Increased stretch receptor firing with decreased sympathetic outflow
Decreased stretch receptor firing with increased vagal outflow
Decreased stretch receptor firing with increased sympathetic outflow
approach: Blood loss lowers arterial pressure, so the arterial wall stretches less.
Less stretch means fewer impulses from the carotid sinus (via cranial nerve IX) and aortic arch (via cranial nerve X) to the medulla.
The medulla responds by reducing vagal tone and raising sympathetic outflow, which speeds the heart and constricts vessels.
questions.why: Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch fire in proportion to arterial wall stretch. A fall in pressure after hemorrhage reduces their firing, which removes their normal inhibition of the vasomotor center. Sympathetic outflow rises and vagal outflow falls, so heart rate, contractility, arteriolar tone, and venous tone all increase. This is why tachycardia with cool, pale skin is an early sign of significant blood loss.
whyNot: Increased stretch receptor firing happens when pressure rises. The extra vagal outflow would slow the heart, which is the response to hypertension.
Increased firing with less sympathetic outflow is also the response to a rise in arterial pressure, the opposite of his situation.
Firing does fall after hemorrhage, but the reflex lowers vagal outflow. Raised vagal outflow would slow his heart.
Correct.

questions.stem: His hemoglobin concentration is near normal even though he has lost a large volume of blood. Which of the following best explains this finding?
options: Erythropoietin has already increased red cell production
Whole blood was lost, so its concentration has not changed yet
Aldosterone has expanded his plasma volume by retaining sodium
Red cells lost into the abdomen have already been reabsorbed
approach: Hemoglobin is a concentration (grams per deciliter), not a total amount.
In acute hemorrhage, cells and plasma are lost together in the same proportion.
Hemoglobin falls only after interstitial fluid shifts into vessels or IV fluid is given, which takes hours.
questions.why: In acute bleeding, red cells and plasma leave together, so the volume falls but the concentration of hemoglobin stays close to baseline at first. Over the next hours, lower capillary hydrostatic pressure pulls interstitial fluid into the capillaries, and IV fluids add more volume, which dilutes the remaining red cells. The full drop in hemoglobin often appears over about 24 to 72 hours. A near normal early hemoglobin therefore does not rule out major hemorrhage, and pulse and blood pressure are better early guides.
whyNot: Erythropoietin rises within hours, but new red cells take several days to reach the blood, seen as a reticulocyte rise at about 3 to 5 days.
Correct.
Aldosterone-driven sodium retention takes hours and adds plasma volume. Any added plasma would dilute red cells and lower hemoglobin, not keep it normal.
Blood in the peritoneal cavity is absorbed slowly over days to weeks, too late to affect a hemoglobin drawn 40 minutes after injury.

questions.stem: The virus that caused his illness two weeks ago enters B cells through CD21. A blood smear at that time showed many large atypical lymphocytes. Which of the following cell types are these atypical lymphocytes most likely to be?
options: Cytotoxic CD8+ T cells reacting to infected B cells
Infected B cells maturing into antibody-secreting plasma cells
CD4+ helper T cells infected through the CD4 molecule
Monocytes that carry viral inclusion bodies
approach: Heterophile-positive infectious mononucleosis is caused by Epstein-Barr virus, which infects B cells through CD21.
The body controls infected B cells with a large cytotoxic T-cell response.
The atypical lymphocytes on the smear are these activated CD8+ T cells.
questions.why: Epstein-Barr virus binds CD21 (complement receptor 2) on B cells and drives them to proliferate. The host responds with a strong expansion of cytotoxic CD8+ T cells that kill infected B cells. These activated T cells are large with abundant cytoplasm that scallops around neighboring red cells, and they are the atypical lymphocytes seen in mononucleosis. The same lymphoid expansion enlarges the spleen and makes it fragile, which is why contact sports are avoided for several weeks after the illness.
whyNot: Correct.
Infected B cells are present, but they make up a small fraction of circulating lymphocytes. The atypical cells are mostly the T cells responding to them.
Infection of CD4+ T cells through the CD4 molecule describes HIV. Epstein-Barr virus targets B cells through CD21.
Monocytes are not the atypical cells in mononucleosis. Large cells with owl-eye inclusions suggest cytomegalovirus infection of tissue cells.

questions.stem: He undergoes splenectomy. A blood smear several weeks later shows erythrocytes containing small, round, dark purple nuclear remnants. Loss of which of the following splenic functions best explains this finding?
options: Production of IgM by marginal zone B cells
Storage of about a third of platelets in the spleen
Removal of red cell inclusions by red pulp macrophages
Synthesis of erythropoietin by splenic interstitial cells
approach: Identify the inclusions as Howell-Jolly bodies, which are DNA remnants in red cells.
Recall that red cells normally squeeze through the cords and sinusoids of the red pulp.
Red pulp macrophages remove inclusions during this passage, so the inclusions persist after splenectomy.
questions.why: Blood entering the red pulp passes through the splenic cords and must squeeze through narrow slits in the sinusoid walls. Macrophages there remove old or damaged red cells and pluck out inclusions such as nuclear remnants, a process called pitting. Without a spleen, red cells keep their Howell-Jolly bodies, so these bodies on a smear are a marker of absent or poorly functioning splenic tissue.
whyNot: Marginal zone B cells make IgM against encapsulated bacteria. Losing them explains the infection risk after splenectomy, not nuclear remnants in red cells.
The spleen holds about a third of the platelet mass. Losing this pool causes a rise in platelet count after splenectomy, not red cell inclusions.
Correct.
Erythropoietin is made mainly by peritubular interstitial cells in the kidney, with a small share from the liver. The spleen is not a source.

topics: Red pulp and white pulp function

dx: Splenic infarction in sickle cell trait at high altitude
case: A 38-year-old man with sickle cell trait develops sudden, sharp left upper quadrant pain on the second day of a ski trip at about 3,000 m (about 9,800 ft) elevation. He has never had a similar episode. Temperature is 37.4 °C (99.3 °F), pulse is 104/min, and blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg. Physical examination shows left upper quadrant tenderness. Lactate dehydrogenase is 410 U/L (140 to 280 U/L). Hemoglobin electrophoresis shows about 38% hemoglobin S and 60% hemoglobin A. Contrast CT shows a wedge-shaped area of the spleen that does not enhance, with its base at the capsule. The diagnosis is splenic infarction.

questions.stem: This splenic infarct is pale. A lung infarct after a pulmonary embolus is usually dark red and hemorrhagic. Which of the following features of the lung best explains this difference?
options: Its arteries are end arteries with no collateral flow
Bronchial arteries keep perfusing the dead tissue
Its cells consume more oxygen than splenic cells do
The embolus also blocks the pulmonary venous outflow
approach: Pale infarcts form in solid organs with end-arterial supply, such as the spleen, kidney, and heart.
Red infarcts form where blood keeps entering the dead tissue.
The lung has a dual supply: pulmonary arteries and bronchial arteries from the systemic circulation.
questions.why: The spleen and kidney are supplied by end arteries, so when one branch is blocked the territory loses its blood and dies pale, in a wedge with its base at the capsule. The lung receives blood from both the pulmonary arteries and the bronchial arteries. After a pulmonary embolus, bronchial blood keeps flowing into the dying, loose lung tissue and leaks out, giving a hemorrhagic red infarct. The same dual supply explains why most pulmonary emboli in healthy lungs do not cause infarction at all.
whyNot: End arteries without collaterals describe the spleen and kidney and lead to pale infarcts. The lung has a dual supply.
Correct.
Oxygen demand affects how fast cells die, but it does not decide whether blood fills the infarct.
A pulmonary embolus lodges in a pulmonary artery and does not block venous outflow, so it cannot explain the blood-filled infarct this way.

topics: Dual blood supply of the lung

questions.stem: If tissue from the infarcted area were examined 2 days after the onset of pain, which of the following microscopic patterns would most likely be seen?
options: Liquefactive necrosis with a cyst forming
Caseous necrosis with surrounding granulomas
Fat necrosis with chalky deposits of calcium soaps
Coagulative necrosis with preserved cell outlines
approach: Identify the cause of cell death: ischemia in a solid organ.
Recall that ischemic death in solid organs other than the brain gives coagulative necrosis.
In coagulative necrosis, proteins denature, so cell outlines and tissue architecture remain while nuclei fade.
questions.why: Ischemia in solid organs such as the spleen, kidney, and heart causes coagulative necrosis. Denaturation of structural proteins and enzymes slows breakdown of the dead cells, so ghost outlines of cells and the basic architecture persist for days while nuclei disappear. Neutrophils gather at the edge of the infarct within 1 to 2 days, and the area is slowly replaced by a fibrous scar.
whyNot: Liquefactive necrosis with cyst formation is the pattern of ischemic infarcts in the brain and of abscesses.
Caseous necrosis with granulomas suggests tuberculosis or some fungal infections, not an ischemic infarct.
Fat necrosis with calcium soaps is typical of acute pancreatitis or trauma to fatty tissue such as the breast.
Correct.

questions.stem: Low oxygen tension at altitude triggered sickling in his spleen. Which of the following molecular events most directly drives the sickling?
options: Unstable globin that precipitates as Heinz bodies
Excess alpha chains that form insoluble aggregates
Valine contacts linking deoxygenated HbS molecules
Spectrin deficiency that makes the membrane rigid
approach: Recall the sickle mutation: a point mutation in the beta-globin gene that replaces glutamate with valine at position 6.
Valine is hydrophobic and, in deoxygenated hemoglobin S, fits into a pocket on a neighboring hemoglobin molecule.
These contacts build long polymers that deform the red cell.
questions.why: Hemoglobin S results from a missense point mutation in the beta-globin gene that places valine instead of glutamate at position 6. When hemoglobin S gives up its oxygen, the hydrophobic valine binds a complementary site on an adjacent molecule, and the molecules stack into long polymers that distort and stiffen the cell. In sickle cell trait, about 40% of hemoglobin is hemoglobin S, so sickling needs severe stress such as high altitude, dehydration, or acidosis. The spleen is vulnerable because blood moves slowly through its red pulp, where oxygen and pH are low.
whyNot: Heinz bodies are precipitated hemoglobin. They form when oxidant stress damages hemoglobin in G6PD deficiency, or with unstable hemoglobin variants. They do not cause sickling.
Excess alpha chains precipitate in beta-thalassemia because too little beta globin is made. They damage red cell precursors and do not form sickle polymers.
Correct.
Spectrin deficiency causes hereditary spherocytosis, where red cells lose membrane and become spheres.

questions.stem: Which of the following would most likely produce a red (hemorrhagic) infarct instead of a pale one like this patient's?
options: Torsion of the testis on its spermatic cord
Embolic occlusion of a renal artery branch
Thrombosis of a coronary artery branch
Atherosclerotic occlusion of a splenic artery branch
approach: Pale infarcts follow arterial occlusion in solid organs with end-arterial supply.
Red infarcts form when blood keeps entering dead tissue, as with venous occlusion.
Torsion twists the cord and compresses the thin-walled veins before the thicker arteries, so blood enters but cannot leave.
questions.why: In testicular torsion the spermatic cord twists. Veins have thin walls and low pressure, so they collapse first while the arteries keep pushing some blood in. The testis becomes congested, then infarcts with blood trapped inside, producing a red infarct. Ovarian torsion and volvulus of the bowel behave the same way, while arterial occlusion in the kidney, heart, and spleen gives pale infarcts.
whyNot: Correct.
The kidney has end arteries, so a branch embolus produces a pale wedge-shaped infarct.
The heart muscle is solid tissue supplied by end arteries, so a coronary thrombosis typically produces a pale infarct.
An occluded splenic artery branch gives a pale infarct like this patient's, since the spleen is supplied by end arteries.

dx: Generalized edema from nephrotic syndrome (minimal change disease)
case: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the clinic because his eyes have been puffy every morning for a week, and now his legs and scrotum are swollen. He had a mild cold 2 weeks ago. Blood pressure is 98/60 mm Hg. Physical examination shows periorbital edema, scrotal edema, and pitting edema of both legs. Urinalysis shows 4+ protein and no red cells. The urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is 6.2 mg/mg (under 0.2 mg/mg). Serum albumin is 1.6 g/dL (3.5 to 5.0 g/dL), total cholesterol is 380 mg/dL (under 170 mg/dL), and serum creatinine is 0.3 mg/dL (0.3 to 0.7 mg/dL). The diagnosis is nephrotic syndrome, most likely minimal change disease, with generalized edema.

questions.stem: Which of the following changes in Starling forces at his systemic capillaries is the main cause of fluid accumulation in his tissues?
options: Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure
Increased capillary permeability to protein
Decreased plasma oncotic pressure
Decreased interstitial hydrostatic pressure
approach: Find the key lab: serum albumin of 1.6 g/dL from heavy urinary protein loss.
Albumin provides most of the plasma oncotic pressure that holds fluid inside capillaries.
With less oncotic pull, net filtration rises and fluid collects in loose tissues such as the eyelids and scrotum.
questions.why: Net filtration across a capillary depends on capillary hydrostatic pressure pushing fluid out and plasma oncotic pressure pulling it back. Albumin supplies most of the plasma oncotic pressure, so heavy proteinuria with a low serum albumin lowers this pull and more fluid stays in the interstitium. Edema shows first where tissue is loose, such as around the eyes in the morning. Renal sodium retention also adds to the edema in nephrotic syndrome, but the low oncotic pressure is the classic Starling explanation.
whyNot: Raised capillary hydrostatic pressure drives edema in heart failure and venous obstruction. Nothing in his case points to high venous pressure.
Increased permeability to protein drives edema in inflammation, burns, and sepsis. The leak in his disease is at the glomerulus, while his systemic capillaries are normal.
Correct.
A fall in interstitial hydrostatic pressure would favor filtration slightly, but it is not the main problem here. Interstitial pressure actually rises as edema fluid collects.

questions.stem: A woman develops chronic arm swelling after removal of her axillary lymph nodes. Compared with this boy's edema fluid, her edema fluid is most likely to have which of the following features?
options: A higher protein concentration
A lower protein concentration
More neutrophils and fibrin strands
Similar protein but more red blood cells
approach: Recall that lymphatics return filtered fluid and the protein that leaks out of capillaries back to the blood.
When lymphatics are blocked, the protein stays behind in the interstitium.
His edema comes from low plasma protein with normal capillaries, so his fluid is a low-protein transudate.
questions.why: Each day about 2 to 3 L of filtered fluid, along with plasma proteins that slowly leak from capillaries, returns to the blood through lymphatics. Lymphatic obstruction, as after axillary node dissection or in filariasis, traps that protein in the tissue, raising interstitial oncotic pressure and producing protein-rich edema that can lead to fibrosis over time. In nephrotic syndrome, plasma albumin is low and capillary walls are intact, so the edema fluid is a protein-poor transudate.
whyNot: Correct.
A lower protein concentration describes his transudate. Lymphatic obstruction does the opposite because protein can no longer be cleared from the tissue.
Neutrophils and fibrin are features of an inflammatory exudate, such as in infection or acute inflammation. Simple lymphatic obstruction is not inflammatory at the start.
Red cells in edema fluid suggest hemorrhage or trauma. Lymphatic obstruction changes protein content, not red cell content.

questions.stem: Three weeks later he develops fever and diffuse abdominal tenderness. Paracentesis yields cloudy ascitic fluid with a neutrophil count of 1,500/µL (under 250/µL). Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause?
options: Staphylococcus aureus
Candida albicans
Clostridioides difficile
Streptococcus pneumoniae
approach: Identify the infection as spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in a child with nephrotic ascites.
Recall that nephrotic children lose IgG and complement factors in the urine, which weakens opsonization.
Choose the encapsulated organism classically linked to peritonitis in nephrotic children.
questions.why: Children with nephrotic syndrome lose IgG and some complement factors in the urine. Encapsulated bacteria resist phagocytosis unless they are coated by antibody and complement, so weak opsonization raises the risk of invasive infection by them. Streptococcus pneumoniae is the classic cause of spontaneous peritonitis in nephrotic children, and gram-negative rods such as Escherichia coli are the other main cause.
whyNot: Staphylococcus aureus causes skin, line, and bone infections. It is an unusual cause of spontaneous peritonitis and is not the organism linked to loss of opsonins here.
Candida peritonitis is mainly seen with bowel perforation, peritoneal dialysis, or long antibiotic courses, not as a spontaneous infection in nephrotic syndrome.
Clostridioides difficile causes colitis after antibiotic use. It does not cause spontaneous peritonitis.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following mechanisms best explains his total cholesterol concentration of 380 mg/dL?
options: Loss-of-function mutation in the LDL receptor gene
Increased hepatic synthesis of apoB lipoproteins
Increased intestinal uptake of dietary cholesterol
Reduced use of cholesterol for bile acid synthesis
approach: Link the hyperlipidemia to the other nephrotic findings: low albumin and low plasma oncotic pressure.
Recall that the liver responds by increasing protein synthesis, including albumin and lipoproteins.
More apoB-containing lipoproteins (VLDL and LDL) leave the liver, so cholesterol rises.
questions.why: In nephrotic syndrome the liver responds to protein loss and low oncotic pressure by making more proteins, including apoB-containing lipoproteins such as VLDL, which becomes LDL. Clearance of lipoproteins is also reduced, partly because lipoprotein lipase activity falls. The combined result is high cholesterol and often high triglycerides, which usually settle once the proteinuria resolves.
whyNot: An LDL receptor mutation causes familial hypercholesterolemia, which is present from birth and would not appear suddenly with proteinuria and edema.
Correct.
Intestinal absorption of cholesterol is not the driver in nephrotic syndrome. The extra lipoproteins come from the liver.
Reduced conversion of cholesterol to bile acids can raise cholesterol, but it is not the mechanism linked to protein loss in nephrotic syndrome.

dx: Acute arterial thrombosis of the superficial femoral artery
case: A 64-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because his right leg suddenly became painful, pale, and cool this morning. For the past year he has had calf pain after walking two blocks. He has type 2 diabetes and a 45-pack-year smoking history. Physical examination shows that the right femoral pulse is present, but the right popliteal and pedal pulses are absent. His heart rhythm is regular, and echocardiography shows no cardiac thrombus. Platelet count is 260,000/µL (150,000 to 400,000/µL). Angiography shows a thrombus on an ulcerated atherosclerotic plaque that blocks the right superficial femoral artery. The diagnosis is acute arterial thrombosis of the superficial femoral artery.

questions.stem: The first step in forming his thrombus was adhesion of platelets to the subendothelium exposed by the ulcerated plaque. Which of the following interactions mediates this adhesion under the high shear stress of arterial flow?
options: Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor binding fibrinogen
Glycoprotein Ib binding von Willebrand factor
P2Y12 receptor binding adenosine diphosphate
Tissue factor binding factor VIIa
approach: Separate the steps of platelet plug formation: adhesion, activation, then aggregation.
Adhesion is the step where a resting platelet first sticks to exposed collagen.
At high arterial shear, von Willebrand factor bound to collagen captures platelets through glycoprotein Ib.
questions.why: When a plaque ulcerates, subendothelial collagen is exposed. Von Willebrand factor from plasma and endothelium binds the collagen and unfolds under the high shear of arterial flow. Platelets then stick to it through their glycoprotein Ib receptor, which is the adhesion step. The adherent platelets activate, release ADP and thromboxane A2, and then aggregate, building a platelet-rich arterial thrombus.
whyNot: Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa binding fibrinogen links platelets to one another. This is aggregation, the step that follows adhesion and activation.
Correct.
ADP binding the P2Y12 receptor amplifies platelet activation and recruits more platelets. It acts after the platelets have already adhered.
Tissue factor binding factor VIIa starts the coagulation cascade that makes thrombin and fibrin. It is not the receptor interaction that makes platelets stick to the vessel wall.

topics: Platelet adhesion and von Willebrand factor

questions.stem: Before today, his leg tolerated a year of gradual narrowing of the superficial femoral artery. Collateral branches of which of the following arteries most likely carried blood around the narrowing to the region of the knee?
options: Obturator artery
Inferior epigastric artery
Superficial circumflex iliac artery
Deep femoral artery
approach: The superficial femoral artery continues as the popliteal artery behind the knee.
Look for an artery that arises above the narrowing and has branches that reach the knee.
The deep femoral (profunda femoris) artery sends perforating branches and the descending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery down to join the genicular arteries.
questions.why: The femoral artery divides into the superficial femoral artery and the deep femoral (profunda femoris) artery. Branches of the deep femoral artery, including its perforating arteries and the descending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery, connect with genicular branches of the popliteal artery around the knee. When the superficial femoral artery narrows slowly, these channels enlarge and carry blood around the blockage. This is why chronic narrowing caused only calf pain on walking, while sudden thrombosis today overwhelmed the collaterals.
whyNot: The obturator artery supplies the medial thigh muscles and the hip. Its branches do not reach the knee anastomosis.
The inferior epigastric artery runs up the anterior abdominal wall and joins the superior epigastric artery. It is a collateral around aortic or iliac blockage, not around the thigh.
The superficial circumflex iliac artery supplies skin near the anterior superior iliac spine and does not reach the knee.
Correct.

questions.stem: He is started on daily aspirin. Which of the following best explains why one dose of aspirin impairs a platelet for the rest of its life span of about 7 to 10 days?
options: Aspirin binds glycoprotein IIb/IIIa for about 10 days
Platelets have no nucleus to make new cyclooxygenase
Aspirin is stored inside platelet dense granules
Platelets lack the enzymes that clear salicylate
approach: Recall the target: aspirin irreversibly acetylates cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1).
Without COX-1, platelets cannot turn arachidonic acid into thromboxane A2, a key signal for aggregation.
A platelet has no nucleus, so it cannot replace the blocked enzyme, and the effect lasts until new platelets are made.
questions.why: Aspirin acetylates a serine in the active site of COX-1, which blocks the enzyme permanently. Platelets use COX-1 to convert arachidonic acid into thromboxane A2, which promotes vasoconstriction and platelet aggregation. Platelets have no nucleus and cannot make meaningful amounts of new enzyme, so each exposed platelet stays inhibited for its life span. Normal function returns only as the marrow releases new platelets, about 10% of the total each day.
whyNot: Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa is blocked by drugs such as abciximab and eptifibatide. Aspirin does not bind this receptor.
Correct.
Dense granules store ADP, calcium, and serotonin. Aspirin is not stored there.
Salicylate is cleared by the liver and kidneys within hours. The lasting effect comes from the permanently acetylated enzyme, not from drug left in the platelet.

questions.stem: He undergoes bypass surgery and receives unfractionated heparin. Six days later his platelet count is 95,000/µL, and a new thrombus forms in a vein of his left arm. Which of the following mechanisms best explains these events?
options: Heparin directly clumps platelets without any antibody
IgE against heparin causes mast cell degranulation
IgG to heparin-platelet factor 4 activates platelets
Heparin depletes antithrombin, leaving thrombin unchecked
approach: Note the timing and pattern: a platelet fall of more than 50% about 5 to 10 days after starting heparin, plus new thrombosis.
This is heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT), an antibody-mediated reaction.
IgG binds heparin-platelet factor 4 complexes, and the immune complexes activate platelets through Fc gamma receptors.
questions.why: In heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, heparin binds platelet factor 4 (PF4) and creates a new antigen. The patient makes IgG against heparin-PF4 complexes, and the antibody-coated complexes bind Fc gamma IIa receptors on platelets and activate them. Activated platelets release procoagulant particles and are cleared, so the count falls while clots form in veins and arteries. The usual onset is about 5 to 10 days after first exposure, the time needed to make IgG.
whyNot: A mild, early fall in platelets from direct heparin effect can occur within the first 1 to 2 days, but it is harmless and does not cause thrombosis.
IgE-mediated reactions cause hives, wheezing, or anaphylaxis, not a falling platelet count with clots.
Correct.
Heparin works by boosting antithrombin. Any small drop in antithrombin does not explain a large fall in platelets.
